node.label: Mary Jane Logan McCallum
node.date_label: 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' 2009 · Indigenous Women, Work, and History 2014 · 'Words for Reading Indigenous Health History' 2017 · 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' 2018 · open letter 2021
node.description: Historian of Indigenous labour, health and archives. Indigenous Women, Work, and History (2014) follows domestic workers, hairdressers, community health representatives and nurses through state placement programmes, 1940–80; her reviewer Carol Williams notes that she worked with nursing associations who 'granted full access to records', and that her conclusion 'reflects on the professional status and glaring absence of Indigenous historians in academia'. Writing in 2018, she treats archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records were made without Indigenous knowledge or consent, yet remain vital to Indigenous history. She describes interpreting such records together with others rather than alone, and hopes for Indigenous roles in making and keeping records. She sits on the managing board of Shekon Neechie.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Mary Jane Logan McCallum (b. 1974); 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' (AIQ, 2009); Indigenous Women, Work, and History, 1940–1980 (UMP, 2014); 'Starvation, Experimentation, Segregation, and Trauma' (CHR, 2017); 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (Shekon Neechie, 2018). Professor of History and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous People, History and Archives, University of Winnipeg.
node.scope_note: Read in full: 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018); Williams's review (BC Studies 191, 2016); the 2021 open letter; the 2020 Lethbridge notice. Unread: Structures of Indifference (with Adele Perry) and Nii Ndahlohke (2022). History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: cited by 44 Canadian History PhDs, rising; context only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records made without consent are read critically and interpreted together with others (2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced; its family material is not used). 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018): opening (archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians); section on Library and Archives Canada (records made under the Indian Act without Indigenous knowledge or consent; still vital to Indigenous history); closing paragraph (an interpretive method that involved other people; restricted records under a researcher agreement). Williams 2016 (BC Studies 191, read in full) on her collaboration with Indigenous nursing associations.

proposed_edges.relationship: Indigenous women's wage work, 1940–80 (domestic workers, hairdressers, community health representatives, nurses) under state placement programmes: Indigenous labour history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UMP contents (chs. 1–4) and description; Williams 2016 (BC Studies 191), who reads the book as of interest to 'students of labour history' and quotes it on 'aboriginal women’s lives inescapably involved in modern labour that was highly regulated by the Canadian nation-state' (p. 239, as quoted by Williams); 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' (AIQ 33:4, 2009; title only).

proposed_edges.relationship: An Indigenous historian's account of the colonial archive: the state at the door, records made without consent, reading them as their makers did, and the case for Indigenous control of records (2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie: cited, not reproduced). 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (2018), section on Library and Archives Canada: security and registration at the national archives; reading Indian Affairs files requires adopting the department's logic; a hope for Indigenous roles in the making, storage and regulation of records, community-based and at LAC. She cites Susan Hill on the Indigenous research trip to the national archives.
